originalGroup.material:
A. A seed’s journey and a shadow clock

A seed may fall close to the plant that produced it, but many plants have ways of sending seeds farther away. The method varies with the seed and its surroundings. Looking at its shape can suggest how a journey might begin.

Some seeds carry light, wing-like parts. A moving stream of air can turn those structures and slow the fall. ____1____ The same breeze therefore has more time to carry the seed sideways before it reaches the ground.

Other seeds have small hooks. ____2____ When an animal later moves away, the seed may travel with it. The attachment need not last forever to change where the seed finally lands.

Fruit offers another route. An animal may eat the fruit and carry seeds away from the parent plant. ____3____ Different fruits and seeds interact with animals in different ways, so one simple account cannot describe every case.

Water can carry some seeds too. Their outer structures may help them float for a period. ____4____ Reaching land is still only one stage; the conditions there must also allow growth.

These journeys do not guarantee that a seed will become a plant. ____5____ Movement changes the possible starting place, but survival depends on what happens after arrival as well as on the journey itself.

B. A seed’s journey and a shadow clock

Our science club built a simple shadow clock in the courtyard. ____1____ (make) one sounded easy, but we first needed a place where a fixed object would cast a shadow for several hours. A patch shaded by the building would not serve our purpose.

The teacher gave us a straight stick and asked us to place ____2____ upright. We checked its position before adding marks around the base. The first line ____3____ (draw) at ten o'clock, with the time written beside it.

We returned every hour, although the changing weather sometimes made the shadow's edge hard to see. There were several ____4____ (occasion) when we could record only an approximate end point. We marked that uncertainty rather than pretending every line was equally precise.

The student ____5____ had kept our notebook compared the results. The marks were not arranged exactly as the numbers on an ordinary clock face. This helped us understand that our model was an observation of one place and day, rather than a ready-made clock for every situation.

By afternoon, we had become ____6____ (good) at taking the measurements. We read the ruler ____7____ (careful) and kept the stick in the same position. The teacher asked us ____8____ (explain) which conditions would matter if another class repeated the task.

Our notes included the date, location and weather. It was ____9____ useful beginning because it connected a visible pattern with questions about how that pattern had been recorded. We left the courtyard tidy, taking all our ____10____ (draw) back to the classroom.

A. Public clocks and repairing a book

Before a small clock could be carried easily, people might depend on a shared clock to coordinate parts of the day. A public clock was therefore more than an object on a tower. It made one account of time visible to people moving through a common space.

Changing habits also changed what people expected from public time. A journey or shift might demand closer coordination than a broad division of the day. ____4____ How precise a clock needed to be depended partly on the activities organised around it.

A. Marks in a margin and two drafts
